title: Platonic Task Arithmetic
claim: Task-induced updates from different models align only moderately, and more than tasks within one model, suggesting a shared underlying component.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmaps, left-to-right, shared viridis colorbar at right
description: Two square heatmaps sit side by side with a single viridis colorbar (0 to 1) on the far right. The left panel is a 6x6 matrix of model families (CLIP, OpenCLIP, MetaCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, EVA-CLIP). Its off-diagonal cosine similarities are moderate, about 0.36 to 0.60, and render teal-green. The right panel is an 8x8 matrix of tasks (EuroSAT, DTD, Cars, GTSRB, MNIST, RESISC45, SVHN, SUN397). Its off-diagonal values are mostly low, from -0.15 to 0.57, and render purple-blue. Bright yellow diagonals with 1.00 mark self-similarity. Each cell carries its numeric value in white or black text. The eye goes first to the yellow diagonals. It then compares the greener left panel with the darker right panel. Axis labels are rotated 45 degrees on the x-axis.
caption: Pairwise cosine similarity between fine-tuning-induced descriptors, flattened to a common $N \times M$ shape. (a) Across models for a fixed task, a $K \times K$ matrix averaged over the eight tasks. (b) Across tasks for a fixed model, an $8 \times 8$ matrix averaged over the six families.
abstract: Distinct pre-trained models specialized for the same task converge to closely similar behavior, yet the parameter updates that produce it share no common coordinate system. Weight-space task arithmetic is therefore confined to a single model, and transporting an update between models requires a structural correspondence. Drawing on Plato's allegory of the cave, we hypothesize that these model-specific updates are shadows cast by one shared, model-agnostic object, the platonic task vector. To make it operational across models of different architectures, we introduce Universal Task Descriptors, matrices whose shape is independent of architecture and embedding dimension, which record a task's functional effect and admit addition and negation as ordinary matrix operations, and we transfer a descriptor into a target in two ways. A single least-squares solve returns a linear operator folded into the target's last layer, and a bank of such operators, one per source and task, realizes any composition as a signed sum of its entries. Alternatively, a low-rank adapter of the target's encoder is trained on the same objective at the price of one optimization per edit. Despite a model-specific residual comparable in norm to the shared component, transfer from another model retains 74 to 80 percent of the gain the target's own descriptors attain. Experiments across six model families, eight tasks and audio-text models confirm both realizations.
